summary: For ages 7–9, teach the rainforest water cycle as a loop that the trees help keep going, powered by the Sun's heat: roots absorb water, leaves release it as vapour (transpiration), the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds above the canopy, and much of the rain falls back onto the forest, while moisture blowing in from the sea also adds rain. The distinctive idea beyond the general water cycle is the biological 'pump': the forest makes much of its own rain. Add the feedback that fewer trees mean less transpiration and can mean less rain, which seeds the later deforestation topic. Use precise vocabulary ('transpiration') and make the cause-and-effect visible and manipulable.
misconceptions: 'All the rain comes from the sea/sky' — the forest itself generates much of its own rain via transpiration.
'Plants only drink water, they don't release it' — leaves transpire large amounts of water vapour.
'Transpiration is the same as respiration/breathing out CO2' — it is water vapour leaving through leaf pores.
'Cutting trees won't change the rain' — fewer trees means less transpiration and less rainfall.
'Clouds form for no reason' — rising vapour cools and condenses into cloud.

activities.title: Run and perturb the forest's rain loop
steps: Watch a forest cross-section where water climbs the trunks from the roots, puffs out of the leaves as vapour, gathers into clouds above the canopy, and falls back as rain onto the same forest.
Follow a single droplet all the way around the loop (roots → leaf → vapour → cloud → rain → roots), stepping through one stage at a time.
Use a 'how many trees?' control to reduce the number of trees, and observe what happens to the vapour, the clouds, and the rain.
Add trees back and describe, in your own words, what happens to the clouds and rainfall.
State the rule you discovered in the model: more trees → more transpiration → more rain; fewer trees → less transpiration → less rain.
activities.insight: The rainforest is not just receiving rain — the trees release water vapour through their leaves (transpiration), which helps form clouds and rain over the forest, so removing trees weakens the rain. This is a feedback loop, not only a one-way supply from the sea.

activities.title: Label the loop and name each stage
steps: Study a circular diagram of the forest water cycle with directional arrows connecting roots → leaves → rising vapour → cloud → rain → back to roots.
Select the leaf and state what happens there, using the word 'transpiration' (water escapes from the leaf as vapour).
For each stage, say in one line what is happening (e.g. 'here the vapour cools and condenses into cloud').
Explain why the arrows form a closed loop rather than a straight line.
activities.insight: The water cycle in a rainforest is a closed loop with named stages, and transpiration is the specific step where water leaves the plant through its leaves as vapour.

activities.title: Predict, test and explain: the bag-on-a-branch investigation
steps: Before testing, predict with a reason: if you seal a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a living plant and leave it in the light, will any water appear inside? Write down your reason.
Carry out (or watch) the investigation and return later to observe the inside of the bag.
Explain where the droplets came from, using the word 'transpiration'.
Answer: Where do the clouds above a rainforest come from, if not only from the sea?
Predict what might happen to the rain if half the forest were cut down, and give your reason.
Predict: if the trees could not transpire at all, how would the forest's rainfall change?
activities.insight: Plants release large amounts of water through their leaves (transpiration); this same process feeds the rainforest's clouds, so losing trees reduces the forest's own rainfall.

activities.title: Order the stages and use the key word
steps: Put the five stages of the loop in the correct order: roots absorb water; leaves transpire; vapour rises; vapour cools and condenses into cloud; rain falls back to the roots.
Complete: 'Water leaves the leaf as vapour by a process called ____.' (transpiration)
Choose and justify the better statement: (a) all the rainforest's rain blows in from the sea; (b) the forest makes much of its own rain through transpiration.
activities.insight: Consolidate the sequence, the term 'transpiration', and the self-rain idea so they can be recalled and explained.

checkQuestion: Rainforests are the rainiest places on Earth. Does ALL that rain blow in from the sea as clouds, or does the forest itself help make its own rain? Tell me which, and then tell me HOW the trees could make rain.
checkAnswer: The forest makes much of its own rain. Trees pull up water through their roots and release it from their leaves as water vapour (transpiration); that moisture rises above the canopy, cools into clouds, and falls back as rain onto the same forest — a self-sustaining loop. So not all the rain blows in from the sea; the forest recycles its own water. That's why cutting down the trees can reduce the rainfall.
